That edge, in the accent color, is the whole feedback edge set: removing it breaks all three cycles, and the card lists it with the topological order of what is left, A, B, D, E, C." width="100%"} A *feedback edge set* breaks every cycle: once its edges are removed, an undirected graph becomes a forest and a directed graph becomes a DAG. The cheapest one answers questions such as which dependencies to drop to make a build order possible, which links to cut so a network has no loops, or which "back" edges to reverse before drawing a directed graph in layers. On an undirected graph the result is exact: it is every edge outside a maximum spanning forest (self-loops and repeated parallel edges included), so the edges kept are the heaviest forest. On a directed graph finding the lightest set is NP-hard, and the result is an approximation (see the Technical Notes); it is always *minimal*, though: putting any one of its edges back would close a cycle. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [weighted]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Whether to use edge weights as the cost of removing each edge. If `None` (default), follows the graph's `weighted` flag; otherwise every edge costs `1`, and the result has as few edges as possible. Weights must be non-negative. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The IDs of the edges to remove, in ascending order. Empty if the graph has no cycle. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If a weight used is negative or NaN. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Undirected: Kruskal's algorithm runs from the heaviest edge down (ties go to the lower edge ID), and the edges it rejects form the set; since the kept forest has the largest possible weight, the removed weight is the smallest, in $O(E \log E)$. Directed: the local-ratio algorithm of Demetrescu and Finocchi (2003). It repeatedly finds a cycle by DFS, lowers the residual weight of each of its edges by the cycle's smallest residual weight, and removes the edges that reach zero. Removed edges are then put back, heaviest first, whenever their target can no longer reach their source. The total weight is at most the optimum times the length of the longest cycle; on small random digraphs it was optimal about 95% of the time and never more than 5/3 of the optimum. Each round removes at least one edge and costs $O(V + E)$, so the directed case is $O(E (V + E))$. This follows NetworkX's proposed `minimum_feedback_edge_set` (PR #8521, not yet merged). ## Examples {.doc-examples} A weighted triangle has one cycle, so the lightest feedback edge set is its lightest edge: ::: {#c536991f .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec triangle = ( ec.Graph(weighted=True) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges([("A", "B", 3.0), ("B", "C", 1.0), ("C", "A", 2.0)]) ) drop = triangle.minimum_feedback_edge_set() pairs = [triangle.get_node_ids_by_edge_id(e) for e in drop] [(triangle.get_label_from_id(s), triangle.get_label_from_id(t)) for s, t in pairs] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [('B', 'C')] ``` ::: ::: In this dependency graph, A, B and C depend on each other in a loop, as do B, D and C. Dropping the single edge from C to A breaks both cycles, after which the graph has a topological order: ::: {#d3a96bc5 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} deps = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E"]) .add_edges( [("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A"), ("B", "D"), ("D", "C"), ("D", "E"), ("E", "C")] ) ) drop = deps.minimum_feedback_edge_set() pairs = [deps.get_node_ids_by_edge_id(e) for e in drop] [(deps.get_label_from_id(s), deps.get_label_from_id(t)) for s, t in pairs] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` [('C', 'A')] ``` ::: :::
